newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels want multinational force to take on Hutus.
newsitem.headline: Rebels want multinational force to take on Hutus.

text.p: A rebel leader said on Thursday he opposed a multinational force being sent to eastern Zaire without the power to separate extremist Rwandan Hutu militiamen from refugees.

"I am opposed to any force that is not neutral, and a force that comes here without a mandate to separate the Interahamwe and the refugees is unfeasible, impractical and useless," rebel chief Laurent Kabila told a news conference in Goma city.
Kabila was refering to Hutu Interahamwe militiamen who helped lead the genocide of up to one million people in Rwanda in 1994 and intimidate refugees in eastern Zaire against returning home.
"I don't see it is clear who is giving this mandate. We have not even been consulted by the United Nations about this," said Kabila.

He did not say rebels would turn against a multinational force arriving without the mandate they wanted. The rebels hold key airports in the border towns of Goma, Bukavu and Uvira which the multinational force would have to secure in order to bring in aid to around one million refugees.

The rebels holding a strip of eastern Zaire are also opposed to French involvement in the international force, arguing France backs Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and supported the Hutu-led government in Rwanda before the genocide.

"France has political ends to feed. They want to maintain a regime we are trying to defeat. We are not opposed to the ideal of humanitarian existence but we must beware of colonial crocodile tears," Kabila said.
Western powers agreeing to contribute troops to the force have stressed it would be a strictly humanitarian mission to help more than one million refugees and displaced Zaireans.

Firing resounded around the teeming Mugunga refugee camp west of Goma for hours on Thursday and Goma residents said they believed the rebels were trying to take on Hutu fighters before the Canadian-led force arrived.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said Africa-bound U.S. troops would be armed to protect themselves but not to conduct combat operations while helping to deliver aid to Rwandan refugees.

Perry told reporters the projected ground force of as many as 1,000 U.S. troops, which will be part of a Canadian-led multinational expedition, would have "robust" rules of engagement to protect themselves.
The head of the U.N.'s food aid arm said force must separate "the bad guys with the guns" from starving refugees or its mission would have to be repeated.

Catherine Bertini, executive director of the World Food Programme), also said while the first step would be seeing that no weapons interfered with humanitarian work, ultimately fighters would have to be disarmed.
